newsitem.title: USA: Lawmaker seeks to cut U.S. aid to Indonesia.
newsitem.headline: Lawmaker seeks to cut U.S. aid to Indonesia.

text.p: Representative Patrick Kennedy plans to introduce a bill this month to cut off U.S. aid to Indonesia because of violations of human rights in East Timor, his spokesman said on Tuesday.

U.S. companies were concerned that the Rhode Island Democrat wanted to impose trade sanctions against Indonesia, but his spokesman, Larry Berman, said he was targeting military and economic aid, not trade.
"We do not want to hurt U.S. businesses who are investors over there. We don't want to put trade sanctions on them," Berman said.
"What we are more interested in doing is sending a message to the government of Indonesia," he said. "We want to get Indonesia to stop abusing human rights."
The U.S. State Department and Amnesty International have listed several cases of human rights violations in East Timor.
Kennedy, working with Virginia Republican Representative Frank Wolf, is seeking support in both parties for the bill he aims to introduce in the week of March 17.

Washington provides about $50 million in annual economic assistance to Indonesia for health, environment, anti-poverty, and regulatory programmes. It also sends about $600,000 in assistance for military training, according to U.S. officials.

Trade between the United States and Indonesia is worth about $6 billion, and several U.S. companies have interests in Indonesia, including Mobil., Atlantic Richfield, Unocal, Freeport-McMoRan Copper & Gold, and Reebok International.
The state of Massachusetts is debating its own legislation to bar companies that do business in Indonesia from doing business with the state.
East Timor has been in turmoil since 1975 when Indonesia occupied then annexed the former Portuguese-ruled territory. The United Nations has never recognised Indonesia's rule.

World awareness of East Timor's problems grew last year when Jose Ramos-Horta and Bishop Carlos Filipe Ximenes Belo were awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for their work to end the conflict with Indonesia.
Ramos-Horta last week urged the United States to press Indonesia to let East Timor vote to determine its future.
